extracted.intended_audience: novelists, students of fiction, and critics of the novel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for creating, presenting, and integrating characters in novels — covering plausibility, psychological depth, relationship to plot/point-of-view, and treatment of basic human facts (birth, food, sleep, love, death).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausible gestures and consistent behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist 'assigns them plausible gestures, and causes them to speak by the use of inverted commas, and perhaps to behave consistently. These word-masses are his characters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be given believable physical gestures, speech, and patterns of behaviour; consistency of behaviour (unless intentionally subverted) helps make them convincing. Example usages and contrasts throughout the essay (e.g., Defoe's Moll) illustrate how concrete detail and consistent action create a sense of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to reveal the hidden life (beyond historical evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It is the function of the novelist to reveal the hidden life at its source: to tell us more about Queen Victoria than could be known…’ — the novelist can go beyond external signs and historical evidence to depict inner life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike the historian, the novelist is permitted (and expected) to invent interior motives, thoughts and passions. Use imaginative reconstruction of inner states rather than relying solely on outward actions; this is a chief function and strength of fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character reality = novelist's complete knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A character in a novel is real when the novelist knows everything about it.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reality for a fictional character derives from the author's full, private knowledge of that person (even if not all of it is told). The reader must sense that the author could answer any question about the character — this implicates depth and internal coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convincingness through conformity to the novel's artistic laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The esthetic reply: 'a character in a novel is real when it lives in accordance with such laws' (i.e., the internal laws of the work of art rather than daily life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters need not mimic daily life exactly; they must be convincing within the rules and purpose of the particular novel. Consistency with the novel's internal logic and tone is as important as literal realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of the five human facts (birth, food, sleep, love, death)
rubrics_metrics.description: The main facts in human life are five: birth, food, sleep, love and death — novels tend to handle these unevenly (birth is rarely explored; death is congenial and often well-handled; food and sleep are usually perfunctory; love is over-emphasized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how you deploy these universal experiences: broaden representation (e.g., explore birth or sleep/dream-life more fully), avoid perfunctory or token treatment, and be cautious about inflating love into the central, constant preoccupation unless that matches the novel's truth. Use each fact deliberately — death suits endings; love is often used as convenient plot closure (marriage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-emphasising love as the novel's dominant activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Love 'has done them harm and made them monotonous' — novelists often make characters unduly sensitive to love, because (a) the novelist's own state leaks into the characters and (b) love conveniently ends books (marriage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't let love occupy implausible proportions of characters' inner lives unless you have reason; avoid defaulting to love/marriage as the easy structuring device or ending. If love is central, justify its centrality by the character's life and the novel's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of characters with plot, moral, atmosphere, and fellow characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters will have to 'adapt themselves to other requirements of their creator' — plot, moral, fellow characters, atmosphere, etc.; in many novels characters are inter-dependent and must exercise mutual restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess characters not in isolation but by how well they function within the novel's network: do they fit the plot, sustain theme, interact plausibly with other figures (Jane Austen's interdependence is the example)? Characters that are too isolated ('trees in a park') may be ill-suited to novels that require ensemble cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat vs round character (depth metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters (types/humours) are constructed around a single idea and can be summed in one sentence; round characters show multiple, sometimes conflicting qualities and approach a 'curve' of complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether a character is meant to be a type (flat) or a complex individual (round). Use the flat character for functional or comic purposes; develop round characters through multiple, sometimes contradictory traits, history and inner life (examples: Mrs. Micawber as flat; Moll as more fully rounded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility and explicability even when not fully explained
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘He may not choose to tell us all he knows… but he will give us the feeling that though the character has not been explained, it is explicable.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A character can omit backstory or private facts, but the reader must feel that the character's actions could be explained coherently. Work toward an impression of internal logic and 'explicability' — avoid characters who act inexplicably without an implied reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between character autonomy and authorial control
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters inside a creation 'try to live their own lives' and often 'run away' or 'get out of hand'; if allowed complete freedom they may 'kick the book to pieces', and if kept too sternly in check they may 'revenge themselves by dying'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage the tension between letting characters surprise you and ensuring they serve the work's needs. Excessive freedom can sabotage structure; excessive control can leave characters dead and the book inert. Find a working balance in which characters feel alive yet coherent with plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view determines visibility of secret life
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'the narrator and the creator are one' the secret life becomes visible; point of view affects how much of a character's inner life is presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a point of view that determines what the reader may know of a character's inner life. First-person or intrusive narration can make secret lives visible; more detached points of view limit what may be revealed. Use POV deliberately to control sympathy and information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid perfunctory recruitment/introduction of characters (born 'off')
rubrics_metrics.description: In many novels a baby 'usually has the air of having been posted' — characters are often introduced perfunctorily and then shelved until needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful how you introduce characters and early life material: avoid mechanical or token introductions that treat characters as mere plot devices. If early life matters, integrate it meaningfully; if not, ensure the later presence still feels grounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensory and quotidian detail (food, dreaming) for verisimilitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Food in fiction is mainly social and characters 'seldom require it physiologically… never digest it unless specially asked'; sleep and dreams are 'perfunctory' and often not realistically rendered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider employing vivid sensory detail (the esthetic side of eating, authentic dream logic) to enrich character and scene. Attention to bodily life and dream-experience can make characters more fully human and avoid the flattened, daylight-only portrait common in many novels.
